newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ wool prices soft in mid-September - Wools of NZ.
newsitem.headline: NZ wool prices soft in mid-September - Wools of NZ.

text.p: The overall price for New Zealand wool fell in mid-September, but some wool types fared better than others, Wools of New Zealand said on Monday.
Prices for superfine merino wool were up substantially, while broader micron merino and halfbred wool prices fell.

In crossbreds, fleece wool prices also eased and skirtings prices were particularly volatile. The market indicator was down four cents to 476 cents on September 12, and fell a further five on September 20 to 471 cents.
Wools of NZ said the trend for full length crossbred fleece had been flat over the past six months, while shorter second shear prices had lifted from their May-June levels.
Finer crossbred full fleece prices ("Chinese types") were still at very low levels, which Wools of NZ said reflected a lack of consistent demand from China.
"There is almost no price premium at present for 33 micron good colour fleece wool over stronger 35 micron wool," it said.

Auction sales of new wool in the first two months of the 1996/97 season were up one percent on a year ago, to 6,600 tonnes. Private wool sales in July were up 42 percent on last year, to 3,200 tonnes, and slipe and sheepskin sales were up 74 percent to 2,300 tonnes.

Exports of wool fibre from New Zealand were up 50 percent in July compared with a year ago, to 15,700 tonnes, but Wools of NZ said the increases for July 1996 could largely be explained by the clearance of carried over wool from the 1995/96 season.
Meanwhile, the Wool Exporters' Council said in a statement that wool exporters were supportive of a united industry body to provide a strong and effective lobby for wool concerns.
Executive manager Nick Nicholson said a sector body could include exporters, brokers, merchants and scouring interests, as well as forming closer links with growers through Wools of NZ.
"Growers have not been alone in feeling the financial ramifications of a depressed international wool market, with all sectors of the industry feeling the squeeze," he said.
Nicholson said he had been instructed by exporters to investigate the possibility of forming such an organisation and to prepare a report for the council by February 1997.
